Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

REFERENCE NOTES
The Harborlight volunteer help desk operates from a shared room behind the North Quay library. Its volunteers answer practical requests from residents, including questions about food deliveries, transport to appointments, and help locating forms. Messages arrive through a web form, a public email address, and a tablet at the library entrance. The desk has no full-time staff. On most afternoons, one volunteer reads incoming messages while another checks the printed rota and the contact list. The code below was copied into a training handout after a volunteer asked how a small routing function might fit into the desk’s intake process.

In April, coordinator Mina Patel began collecting examples for a short orientation session. She asked volunteers to use invented names when demonstrating the intake screen, because real requests can contain private details. The examples were written on paper cards before being typed into a practice queue. Mina said, “The point is to understand what the little function can tell us, not to guess what a person meant.” The cards include different message ages, urgency labels, and combinations of those fields. They were not intended to represent every kind of request the desk receives.

The practice queue is separate from the live mailbox. It is displayed on an old laptop with a narrow screen, and a volunteer can see only a few rows at a time. The labels in the queue are used for discussion; they do not send a message to a real responder. During the session, volunteers compare the label from the example function with the words on each card. They also note when the card does not provide enough information to tell how a real message should be handled. The current exercise uses only the short function reproduced below, rather than the desk’s other intake materials.

Several volunteers described different situations while reviewing the cards. Ravi, who usually works at the library table, said that messages about a missed bus sometimes arrive after the trip is over, while a request for tomorrow’s ride can still be useful to act on. He did not suggest that the function knows which event has passed. Elise, who monitors the email inbox on Thursdays, said that people sometimes mark a message urgent because they are worried, even when the request is not time-sensitive. Mina wrote these comments in the session notebook as examples of questions the volunteers might ask when comparing the code with their day-to-day work.

The session took place on a Tuesday, with twelve volunteers attending in two groups. Before the first group arrived, Mina printed copies of the function and placed them beside the blank practice cards. The library’s public computer was unavailable that afternoon, so the groups did not test anything in the actual queue. They talked through sample values aloud and wrote possible cases on the board. When a volunteer asked whether an empty age field should be treated as zero, Mina replied, “Let’s stick to what the snippet itself shows, and mark anything else as a question.” No system behavior beyond the printed code was demonstrated.

The notes from the board were transcribed as follows:
1. Use one card with an urgent value and an age below the number shown in the code.
2. Compare it with a card that has the same age but a different urgency value.
3. Include an age equal to the boundary and one above it, without assuming what units the age uses.
4. Ask what happens when a card leaves out the age field, and distinguish that from a card whose age is written as zero.

On the second group’s cards, the volunteers used the fictional names Jo Alvarez, Sam Okafor, and Tessa Lin. Jo’s card described a message marked urgent with an age of 17. Sam’s card described a message marked urgent with an age of 42. Tessa’s card had an age of 9, but the urgency box was left blank. These were just examples prepared for discussion; the notes do not record outputs from running the function. A separate card said “urgent, age missing,” and one volunteer asked whether the code treated that case the same as an explicit zero. The group left the question beside the code rather than adding an answer to the card.

The coordinators planned to keep the exercise small enough for new volunteers to complete in about fifteen minutes. Each person could mark one point in the handout that seemed clear and one point that they wanted to ask about. Mina collected the handouts after each group, but she did not tally the marks that day. A volunteer named Peter Ng suggested adding a note that a queue label is not the same as a decision about who will respond. Mina copied that suggestion into the notebook, without changing the function or the practice cards.

def route_message(message):
    if message.get('urgent') and message.get('age', 0) < 42:
        return 'priority'
    return 'standard'

At the end of the session, Mina wrote that the printed example should stay attached to the discussion notes so later groups could see exactly which code they were talking about. She also recorded a practical condition for a future exercise: if the library room is unavailable, the orientation can still use the paper cards, but volunteers should not describe the examples as results from the live queue. The next orientation date had not been set. The notebook contains no decision about changing the function, adopting a new routing policy, or sending any of the practice messages to staff.
